arXiv:2610.25533v1 [cs.CV] 18 Oct 2026

Modaliff: A Unified Token Diffusion Model for Any-to-Any Generation

Duc Kieu    Kien Do    Minh Khoa Le    Tung Kieu    Dang Nguyen    Thin Nguyen
Abstract

Any-to-any generation seeks a single model that translates flexibly among text, image, and audio, yet existing approaches either require fully aligned multimodal tuples or a shared representation that suppresses modality-specific structure. We introduce Modaliff, a novel token-based diffusion model that learns from widely available bimodal pairs while preserving each modality in its native latent sequence. Modaliff assembles conditions and targets into a unified token sequence, with per-token attributes to disambiguate token identities and role-based positional embedding to preserve each modality’s internal structure across sequence layouts. This design enables a single denoiser to support diverse generation tasks without task-specific architectural changes or a shared cross-modal latent space. Beyond one-to-one generation, Modaliff supports multiple conditions either by combining single-condition predictions at inference or by lightweight finetuning on captions that jointly describe multiple inputs. Experiments across text, image, and audio show that Modaliff achieves the best fidelity among any-to-any models on most generation tasks while using substantially fewer parameters and training data.

1Applied Artificial Intelligence Initiative, Deakin University

2VinSmart Future, 3Aalborg University

1 Introduction

A long-standing goal of generative modeling is to build a single model that translates freely among text, image, and audio, such as captioning a photograph, imagining the scene behind a sound, or synthesizing audio from a description. Recent diffusion and flow-based models have brought this any-to-any goal closer (Bao et al. 2023b; Tang et al. 2023; Li et al. 2025), building on progress in text-to-image (Rombach et al. 2022) and text-to-audio (Liu et al. 2023a) generation. Yet flexible and efficient any-to-any generation remains challenging because different modalities have fundamentally different structures, with text is sequential and symbolic, image is spatially structured, and audio is temporally continuous.

Existing any-to-any diffusion models typically follow one of two approaches. The first approach, exemplified by UniDiffuser (Bao et al. 2023b) and OmniFlow (Li et al. 2025), concatenates tokens from all modalities and model their joint density over concatenated multimodal tokens with a single transformer. This design is general, but it often requires fully aligned multimodal tuples, which are scarce in practice, and is less flexible for conditional tasks such as Image + Text →\rightarrow Image. The second, represented by CoDi (Tang et al. 2023) and FlowBind (Cha et al. 2026), instead maps all modalities into a shared representation space and condition generation there. This reduces the tuple requirement, but it either requires contrastive pretraining or forces all modalities into the same vector format, limiting representation expressivity.

We introduce Modaliff, a novel token-based diffusion model for any-to-any generation that learns from widely available bimodal pairs without requiring fully aligned multimodal tuples or a shared cross-modal latent space. Our key idea is to represent each modality as a latent token sequence and assemble condition and target modalities into a unified token sequence across generation tasks. To this end, each token of the sequence carries a rich attribute tuple that specifies its modality (e.g., text, image, or audio), role (source or target), and noise level. A role-based positional embedding further organizes token positions across task-varying sequence layouts. Together, these components allow a single denoiser to support flexible source and target combinations without architectural modification, while preserving expressive conditioning through attention over native token sequences.

Beyond one-to-one generation, Modaliff supports multiple conditions through two complementary mechanisms, namely inference-time score composition and lightweight caption-based adaptation. Score composition adopts a product-of-experts formulation to combine the single-condition predictions learned from paired data, enabling multi-condition generation without additional training. In contrast, caption-based adaptation expresses the joint semantics of multiple conditions in language and finetunes Modaliff on a compact set of examples constructed from existing paired data, better capturing interactions among conditions.

Extensive experiments across text, image, and audio demonstrate that Modaliff achieves the best fidelity among any-to-any models on most generation tasks. Compared to OmniFlow and CoDi, Modaliff uses six to eight times fewer parameters and about 5% of OmniFlow’s training data while maintaining competitive results.

Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose Modaliff, an any-to-any diffusion model that learns from bimodal paired data while preserving each modality in its native latent token space. To our knowledge, Modaliff is the first any-to-any model that requires neither a shared cross-modal representation nor fully aligned multimodal tuples for training.

  • •

    We develop two approaches for multi-condition generation through inference-time score composition and lightweight adaptation on caption-based supervision.

  • •

    Across text, image, and audio, Modaliff achieves the best fidelity among any-to-any models on most generation tasks while using substantially fewer parameters and less training data than OmniFlow and CoDi.

2 Background

2.1 Diffusion Models

In diffusion models (Sohl-Dickstein et al. 2015; Song and Ermon 2019; Ho, Jain, and Abbeel 2020; Song, Meng, and Ermon 2021), a clean sample xx is progressively corrupted by Gaussian noise through a predefined process:

xt=at​x+σt​ϵ,ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)x_{t}=a_{t}x+\sigma_{t}\epsilon,\ \ \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\mathrm{I}\right) (1)

where ata_{t} decreases from 1 to 0 and σt\sigma_{t} increases from 0 to 1 as tt goes from 00 to TT.

The generative (reverse) process starts from xT∼𝒩⁡(0,I)x_{T}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\mathrm{I}\right) and iteratively denoises using pθ​(xt−1|xt)p_{\theta}\left(x_{t-1}|x_{t}\right) – a Gaussian transition whose mean depends on the network ϵθ\epsilon_{\theta} that predicts the noise. The model is trained with the denoising objective:

ℒDM​(θ)=𝔼x,t,ϵ​[‖ϵθ​(xt,t)−ϵ‖22]\mathcal{L}_{\text{DM}}\left(\theta\right)=\mathbb{E}_{x,t,\epsilon}\left[\left\|\epsilon_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right)-\epsilon\right\|^{2}_{2}\right] (2)

For conditional generation, classifier-free guidance (CFG) is usually applied:

ϵ~θ​(xt,t,y)=w​ϵθ​(xt,t,y)+(1−w)​ϵθ​(xt,t,∅)\tilde{\epsilon}_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t,y\right)=w\epsilon_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t,y\right)+\left(1-w\right)\epsilon_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t,\varnothing\right) (3)

where ϵθ​(xt,t,y)\epsilon_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t,y\right) and ϵθ​(xt,t,∅)\epsilon_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t,\varnothing\right) are the conditional and unconditional noise predictions, and ww controls the guidance.

2.2 Diffusion Router

Diffusion Router (DR) (Kieu et al. 2026) is a variant of diffusion models designed for the Universal Multi-Domain Translation (UMDT) problem. Given K−1K-1 paired datasets 𝒟k,c={(xk,xc)}n=1Nk\mathcal{D}_{k,c}=\left\{\left(x^{k},x^{c}\right)\right\}^{N_{k}}_{n=1} between a central domain XcX^{c} and K−1K-1 non-central domains XkX^{k} (k≠ck\neq c), DR trains a unified noise predictor ϵθ​(xttgt,t,xsrc,tgt,src)\epsilon_{\theta}\left(x^{\text{tgt}}_{t},t,x^{\text{src}},\text{tgt},\text{src}\right) which supports bidirectional central-noncentral translations Xc↔XkX^{c}\leftrightarrow X^{k} using the objective:

ℒpair​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{pair}}\left(\theta\right) =𝔼(xk,xc)∼𝒟k,c,t,ϵ,ζ[ζ‖ϵθ(xtk,t,xc,k,c)−ϵ‖22\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\left(x^{k},x^{c}\right)\sim\mathcal{D}_{k,c},t,\epsilon,\zeta}\bigg[\zeta\left\|\epsilon_{\theta}\left(x^{k}_{t},t,x^{c},k,c\right)-\epsilon\right\|^{2}_{2}
+(1−ζ)‖ϵθ(xtc,t,xk,c,k)−ϵ‖22],\displaystyle\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ +\left(1-\zeta\right)\left\|\epsilon_{\theta}\left(x^{c}_{t},t,x^{k},c,k\right)-\epsilon\right\|^{2}_{2}\bigg], (4)

At inference, DR can translate between two non-central domains XiX^{i}, XjX^{j} indirectly via the central domain XcX^{c}. To enable direct translation, an additional objective is introduced:

ℒunpair​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{unpair}}\left(\theta\right) =𝔼xtj∼p⁡(xtj|xc)[‖ϵθ(xtj,t,xi,j,i)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x^{j}_{t}\sim p\left(x^{j}_{t}|x^{c}\right)}\left[\left\|\epsilon_{\theta}\left(x^{j}_{t},t,x^{i},j,i\right)\right.\right.
−sg(ϵθ(xtj,t,xc,j,c))‖22],\displaystyle\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \left.\left.-\text{sg}\left(\epsilon_{\theta}\left(x^{j}_{t},t,x^{c},j,c\right)\right)\right\|^{2}_{2}\right], (5)

where sg​(⋅)\text{sg}\left(\cdot\right) denotes the stop gradient operator. The final training objective is:

ℒfinal​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{final}}\left(\theta\right) =λ1​ℒunpair​(θ)+λ2​ℒpair​(θ)\displaystyle=\lambda_{1}\mathcal{L}_{\text{unpair}}\left(\theta\right)+\lambda_{2}\mathcal{L}_{\text{pair}}\left(\theta\right) (6)

Despite promising results, DR is primarily designed for image-to-image translation, assuming all domains share the same dimensionality. This limits its applicability to multimodal settings, where domains may differ in representation and structure. In addition, DR focuses on pairwise translation and does not naturally support composing multiple conditions for generation.

3 Modaliff

3.1 Unified Token-based Representation

A fundamental challenge in multimodal generation is that latent representations of different modalities differ substantially in both structure and semantic abstraction. Existing unified diffusion and flow models typically address this heterogeneity either by modeling a joint distribution over concatenated multimodal tokens (Bao et al. 2023b; Li et al. 2025) or by mapping modalities into a shared representation space (Tang et al. 2023; Cha et al. 2026). The former often requires fully aligned multimodal datasets (Li et al. 2025) and struggles to support flexible conditioning patterns such as Image + Text →\rightarrow Image, while the latter typically discards modality-specific structure and restricts cross-modal interaction to operations between fixed-dimensional vectors.

To address these limitations, we represent each modality as its native latent token sequence and concatenate arbitrary condition and target modalities into a unified sequence. Specifically, let ℳ={1,…,K}\mathcal{M}=\left\{1,\ldots,K\right\} denote the modality set, instantiated with text, image, and audio, following prior multimodal settings (Cha et al. 2026). For each modality i∈ℳi\in\mathcal{M}, a frozen encoder Enci​(⋅)\text{Enc}^{i}\left(\cdot\right) encodes a sample xix^{i} to a token sequence, zi=Enci​(xi),zi∈ℝNi×diz^{i}=\text{Enc}^{i}\left(x^{i}\right),z^{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{i}\times d_{i}}, where NiN_{i} and did_{i} denote the number and dimensionality of tokens. Given a generation task, let 𝒞,𝒯⊆ℳ\mathcal{C},\mathcal{T}\subseteq\mathcal{M} denote the condition and target modality sets, respectively. We concatenate the token sequences of the context and target set as:

Ht=\displaystyle H_{t}= ℋ⁡({zi}i∈𝒞,{ztj}j∈𝒯)\displaystyle\mathcal{H}\left(\left\{z^{i}\right\}_{i\in\mathcal{C}},\left\{z^{j}_{t}\right\}_{j\in\mathcal{T}}\right)
=\displaystyle= Concat​({zi⋅Wini}i∈𝒞,{ztj⋅Winj}j∈𝒯),\displaystyle\text{Concat}\left(\left\{z^{i}\cdot W^{i}_{\text{in}}\right\}_{i\in\mathcal{C}},\left\{z^{j}_{t}\cdot W^{j}_{\text{in}}\right\}_{j\in\mathcal{T}}\right), (7)

where Wini∈ℝdi×dW^{i}_{\text{in}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{i}\times d} is a trainable projection matrix. Here, each condition modality i∈𝒞i\in\mathcal{C} contributes clean sequence ziz^{i}, while each target modality j∈𝒯j\in\mathcal{T} contributes a noisy sequence ztjz^{j}_{t} at diffusion timestep tt, following Eq. 1. This design reduces flexible generation to rearranging condition and target segments, while the shared network and modality-native representations remain unchanged.

Processing all tasks through a unified sequence introduces two challenges. First, HtH_{t} does not specify each token’s modality, condition or target status, or diffusion timestep, leaving the generation task ambiguous to the shared model. Second, the sequence length and segment layout vary across tasks, making conventional positional indexing unsuitable. Global indexing over HtH_{t} (Bao et al. 2023b) binds modalities to a fixed segment order, limiting flexibility, whereas local indexing avoids this constraint but creates artificial correspondences between unrelated tokens sharing the same index, introducing false positional biases into the model.

To resolve the first challenge, we define an attribute tuple (r,i,t)\left(r,i,t\right) for each token, encoding its generation role, modality type, and diffusion timestep. Specifically, r∈{0,1}r\in\left\{0,1\right\}, where r=0r=0 denotes a condition token and r=1r=1 denotes a target token, i∈ℳi\in\mathcal{M} identifies the modality type, and tt records its noise level, with t=0t=0 for clean condition tokens and tt set to the current denoising timestep for target tokens. These attributes are embedded and injected into each transformer block through a token-wise AdaLN (Peebles and Xie 2023), which produces token-specific scale, shift, and gating parameters, enabling the shared network to adapt its computation to each token without modality-specific branches.

We address the second challenge with role-based positional embedding (PE) built on RoPE (Su et al. 2024), in which the positions used in attention depend on whether the attending token belongs to a condition or target segment. Condition queries use local positions and attend only within their own segment, preserving internal structure and avoiding false correspondences across conditions. Target queries retain local target positions while treating all condition segments as an unordered set under a shared positional reference, removing spurious cross-segment biases and supporting flexible condition-target layouts.

Fig. 1 illustrates the overall pipeline, transformer block, and per-token attributes with role-based positional encoding.

3.2 Learning Any-to-Any with Paired Data

Training Objective

We adopt the training objective of DR (Eq. 4) to learn all one-to-one mappings directly from paired datasets. For any two modalities i,j∈ℳi,j\in\mathcal{M} with a paired dataset 𝒟i,j\mathcal{D}_{i,j}, Modaliff learns both denoising directions, i→ji\to j and j→ij\to i, through a symmetric objective:

ℒpair​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{pair}}\left(\theta\right) =𝔼(xi,xj),t,ϵ,ζ[ζ‖zθ(zti,t,zj)−zi‖22\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\left(x^{i},x^{j}\right),t,\epsilon,\zeta}\left[\zeta\left\|z_{\theta}\left(z^{i}_{t},t,z^{j}\right)-z^{i}\right\|^{2}_{2}\right.
+(1−ζ)‖zθ(ztj,t,zi)−zj‖22],\displaystyle\ \ \ \ \ \ +\left.\left(1-\zeta\right)\left\|z_{\theta}\left(z^{j}_{t},t,z^{i}\right)-z^{j}\right\|^{2}_{2}\right], (8)

where ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\mathrm{I}\right), t∼𝒰⁡(1,T)t\sim\mathcal{U}\left(1,T\right), ζ∼ℬ⁡(0.5)\zeta\sim\mathcal{B}(0.5), and zti=at​zi+σt​ϵz^{i}_{t}=a_{t}z^{i}+\sigma_{t}\epsilon . Here, zθ​(zti,t,zj)z_{\theta}\left(z^{i}_{t},t,z^{j}\right) abbreviates Modaliff’s clean-latent prediction, computed on the unified sequence ℋ⁡(zj,zti)\mathcal{H}\left(z^{j},z^{i}_{t}\right) of Eq. 7. The output tokens of the target segment, denoted h^θi∈ℝNi×d\hat{h}^{i}_{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{i}\times d} , are projected back to the native latent space as:

zθ​(zti,t,zj)=h^θi⋅Wouti,Wouti∈ℝd×diz_{\theta}\left(z^{i}_{t},t,z^{j}\right)=\hat{h}^{i}_{\theta}\cdot W^{i}_{\text{out}},\ \ \ W^{i}_{\text{out}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{i}} (9)

where WoutiW^{i}_{\text{out}} is a trainable output projection matrix. Unlike the noise-prediction in Eq. 4, Modaliff predicts the clean latents, which is more robust across heterogeneous pretrained latents with varying scales and heavy-tailed dimensions that can destabilize noise prediction, as shown in Appdx. B.2. During training, we replace the condition with a null token ∅\varnothing with probability 0.20.2, enabling CFG (Ho and Salimans 2021).

To generate xix^{i} from xjx^{j}, we encode zj=Encj​(xj)z^{j}=\text{Enc}^{j}\left(x^{j}\right), initialize zTi∼𝒩⁡(0,I)∈ℝNi×diz^{i}_{T}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\mathrm{I}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{i}\times d_{i}}, assemble ℋ⁡(zj,zTi)\mathcal{H}\left(z^{j},z^{i}_{T}\right), and run diffusion sampler (Song, Meng, and Ermon 2021) with CFG (Eq. 3) in the noise space with ϵθ(zti,t,⋅)=(zti−atzθ(zti,t,⋅))/σt\epsilon_{\theta}\left(z^{i}_{t},t,\cdot\right)=\left(z^{i}_{t}-a_{t}z_{\theta}\left(z^{i}_{t},t,\cdot\right)\right)/\sigma_{t}. The final prediction z^i\hat{z}^{i} is decoded with the frozen decoder, i.e., xi=Deci​(z^i)x^{i}=\text{Dec}^{i}\left(\hat{z}^{i}\right).

Learning with Missing Pairwise Data

In practice, some modality pairs are difficult to collect and provide far less supervision than others. For example, image-audio dataset (𝒟i,j\mathcal{D}_{i,j}) (Chen et al. 2020) are typically scarce compared with image-text (𝒟i,c\mathcal{D}_{i,c}) (Schuhmann et al. 2022) and audio-text (𝒟j,c\mathcal{D}_{j,c}) datasets (Gemmeke et al. 2017), in which case Modaliff can exploit the shared text modality cc to learn the missing Xj↔XiX^{j}\leftrightarrow X^{i} mappings. To learn Xj→XiX^{j}\to X^{i} (or similarly Xj←XiX^{j}\leftarrow X^{i}) without access to 𝒟i,j\mathcal{D}_{i,j}, we reformulate Eq. 5 under clean-latent prediction as:

ℒunpairj→i(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{{}^{j\rightarrow i}}_{\text{unpair}}\left(\theta\right) =𝔼(xj,xc),t,zti∼pθ​(zti|zc)[‖zθ(zti,t,zj)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\left(x^{j},x^{c}\right),t,z^{i}_{t}\sim p_{\theta}\left(z^{i}_{t}|z^{c}\right)}\left[\left\|z_{\theta}\left(z^{i}_{t},t,z^{j}\right)\right.\right.
−sg(zθ(zti,t,zc))‖22],\displaystyle\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \left.\left.-\text{sg}\left(z_{\theta}\left(z^{i}_{t},t,z^{c}\right)\right)\right\|^{2}_{2}\right], (10)

where sg​(⋅)\text{sg}\left(\cdot\right) denotes stop gradient. We jointly optimize Eq. 8 and Eq. 10 via Eq. 6, enabling Xj→XiX^{j}\to X^{i} without 𝒟i,j\mathcal{D}_{i,j}.

Multi-Condition Generation via Score Composition

Modaliff enables multi-condition generation by composing the single-condition predictions learned from pairwise training. Let ii denote the target modality and 𝒮⊆(ℳ∖i)\mathcal{S}\subseteq\left(\mathcal{M}\setminus i\right) the conditioning modalities. Assuming the conditions are conditionally independent given the noisy target, i.e., p⁡({zj}j∈𝒮∣zti)=∏j∈𝒮p⁡(zj∣zti)p\left(\left\{z^{j}\right\}_{j\in\mathcal{S}}\mid z^{i}_{t}\right)=\prod_{j\in\mathcal{\mathcal{S}}}p(z^{j}\mid z^{i}_{t}), the product-of-experts formulation (Nguyen et al. 2025) yields multi-condition noise prediction as:

ϵ~θ​(zti,t,{zj}j∈𝒮)=ϵθ​(zti,t,∅)+∑j∈𝒮wj​[ϵθ​(zti,t,zj)−ϵθ​(zti,t,∅)],\tilde{\epsilon}_{\theta}\left(z^{i}_{t},t,\left\{z^{j}\right\}_{j\in\mathcal{S}}\right)=\epsilon_{\theta}\left(z^{i}_{t},t,\varnothing\right)+\\ \sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}}w_{j}\left[\epsilon_{\theta}\left(z^{i}_{t},t,z^{j}\right)-\epsilon_{\theta}\left(z^{i}_{t},t,\varnothing\right)\right], (11)

where ϵθ(zti,t,⋅)=(zti−atzθ(zti,t,⋅))/σt\epsilon_{\theta}\left(z^{i}_{t},t,\cdot\right)=\left(z^{i}_{t}-a_{t}z_{\theta}\left(z^{i}_{t},t,\cdot\right)\right)/\sigma_{t} and {wj}j∈𝒮\left\{w_{j}\right\}_{j\in\mathcal{S}} control the contribution of each condition. Eq. 11 extends single-condition predictions to multi-condition generation without training on fully aligned multimodal datasets and reduces to standard CFG when only one condition is provided.

3.3 Improving Multi-Condition Generation via Caption-Based Finetuning

Score composition (Eq. 11) enables inference-time multi-condition generation but limits the ability to capture interactions among conditions and struggles with tasks such as (Xi+Xj)→Xi\left(X^{i}+X^{j}\right)\to X^{i}, where the required same-modality prediction ϵθ​(zti,t,zi)\epsilon_{\theta}\left(z^{i}_{t},t,z^{i}\right) is unavailable. To mitigate the gap, we propose a novel approach that constructs a compact finetuning set for multi-condition generation and uses it to adapt Modaliff. Our key idea is to encode joint semantics of multiple conditions in language and transfer them through the text-to-target mappings learned from one-to-one training. For example, image generation from image and audio conditions can be reframed as text-to-image generation using a caption that combines semantics of both conditions.

Formally, we consider two-condition generation (Xi+Xj)→Xk\left(X^{i}+X^{j}\right)\rightarrow X^{k}, with i,j,k∈ℳi,j,k\in\mathcal{M}, following prior any-to-any settings (Tang et al. 2023; Li et al. 2025). Given two pairs (xi,xc)∼𝒟i,c\left(x^{i},x^{c}\right)\sim\mathcal{D}_{i,c} and (xj,x′c)∼𝒟j,c\left(x^{j},x^{\prime c}\right)\sim\mathcal{D}_{j,c}, where cc denotes text, an instruction-tuned language model (Yang et al. 2025) merges xcx^{c} and x′cx^{\prime c} into a natural joint description x~c\tilde{x}^{c} that preserves information from both xix^{i} and xjx^{j}, yielding a finetuning triplet (xi,xj,x~c)\left(x^{i},x^{j},\tilde{x}^{c}\right). Random pairing, however, provides a poor finetuning signal because unrelated captions yield unnatural descriptions, while near-duplicate captions contribute limited complementary information. We therefore compute their cosine similarity as:

sim​(xc,x′c)=⟨Emb​(xc),Emb​(x′c)⟩‖Emb​(xc)‖2​‖Emb​(x′c)‖2,\text{sim}\left(x^{c},x^{\prime c}\right)=\frac{\left\langle\text{Emb}\left(x^{c}\right),\text{Emb}\left(x^{\prime c}\right)\right\rangle}{\left\|\text{Emb}\left(x^{c}\right)\right\|_{2}\left\|\text{Emb}\left(x^{\prime c}\right)\right\|_{2}}, (12)

where Emb​(⋅)\text{Emb}\left(\cdot\right) denotes a sentence-embedding model (Reimers and Gurevych 2019), and retain only pairs satisfying sim​(xc,x′c)∈[γmin,γmax]\text{sim}\left(x^{c},x^{\prime c}\right)\in\left[\gamma_{\text{min}},\gamma_{\text{max}}\right], where γmin\gamma_{\text{min}} and γmax\gamma_{\text{max}} control the similarity range. The resulting triplets supervise task (Xi+Xj)→Xk\left(X^{i}+X^{j}\right)\rightarrow X^{k} with the objective:

ℒmulti(i+j)→k​(θ)=𝔼(xi,xj,x~c),z¯k,ztk​[‖zθ​(ztk,t,{zi,zj})−z¯k‖22],{\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{\left(i+j\right)\rightarrow k}_{\text{multi}}\left(\theta\right)=\mathbb{E}_{\left(x^{i},x^{j},\tilde{x}^{c}\right),\bar{z}^{k},z^{k}_{t}}\left[\left\|z_{\theta}\left(z^{k}_{t},t,\left\{z^{i},z^{j}\right\}\right)-\bar{z}^{k}\right\|^{2}_{2}\right],}

 (13)
s.t. {k=c:ztk=at​z~c+σt​ϵ,z¯k=z~ck≠c:ztk∼pθ​(ztk∣z~c),z¯k=sg​(zθ​(ztk,t,z~c))\text{s.t.\ }\begin{cases}k=c:&z^{k}_{t}=a_{t}\tilde{z}^{c}+\sigma_{t}\epsilon,\ \ \ \ \bar{z}^{k}=\tilde{z}^{c}\\ k\neq c:&z^{k}_{t}\sim p_{\theta}\left(z^{k}_{t}\mid\tilde{z}^{c}\right),\ \ \bar{z}^{k}=\text{sg}\left(z_{\theta}\left(z^{k}_{t},t,\tilde{z}^{c}\right)\right)\end{cases} (14)

where z~c=Encc​(x~c)\tilde{z}^{c}=\text{Enc}^{c}\left(\tilde{x}^{c}\right). To preserve the pretrained one-to-one mappings and finetune efficiently, we optimize Eq. 13 using LoRA (Hu et al. 2022).

4 Experiments

4.1 Experiment Setup

Training Datasets

For image-text dataset, we train Modaliff on 800K pairs sampled from LAION-Aesthetics +6.25 (Schuhmann et al. 2022), replacing noisy captions containing URLs or HTML fragments with captions generated by LLaVA (Liu et al. 2023b). For audio-text dataset, we use 92K human-annotated pairs from AudioCaps v2 (Kim et al. 2019). Although Modaliff does not strictly require image-audio pairs, we include 184K image-audio pairs from VGGSound (Chen et al. 2020) for fair comparison with baselines. We additionally train a variant without VGGSound to assess image↔\leftrightarrowaudio generation through text as the shared modality. Full dataset details are provided in Appx. A.1.

Implementation Details

We use CLIP-ViT-L16 (Radford et al. 2021) to encode an image into zimg∈ℝ1×768z^{\text{img}}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times 768} and Stable-UnCLIP-small (Ramesh et al. 2022) to decode zimgz^{\text{img}}. For text, we build an encoder based on Qwen3-0.6B Embedding (Zhang et al. 2025) to map each text sequence to a fixed-length latent ztxt∈ℝ32×256z^{\text{txt}}\in\mathbb{R}^{32\times 256}, and use a fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B (Yang et al. 2025) to generate text from ztxtz^{\text{txt}}. Appx. A.2 provides details of the text encoder and text decoder. For audio, we use CLAP-HTSAT (Wu et al. 2023) to encode each 10-second waveform into zaud∈ℝ1×512z^{\text{aud}}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times 512} and AudioLDM-S (Liu et al. 2023a) to decode zaudz^{\text{aud}}. Modality-specific encoders and decoders are frozen during training.

Following DiT-L (Peebles and Xie 2023), Modaliff uses 24 transformer blocks, hidden dimension d=1024d=1024, and 16 attention heads, yielding 558M trainable parameters to fit a H100 80GB GPU. We train Modaliff with Eq. 8 for up to 500K iterations with a batch size of 512, bfloat16 precision, and a constant learning rate of 3e-5 with 5K warmup steps. With no VGGSound setting, we finetune Modaliff following Sec. 3.2 to enable image↔\leftrightarrowaudio generation, with reduced learning rate of 5e-6, and λ1=λ2=1\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}=1 in Eq. 6, as recommended by DR (Kieu et al. 2026). For multi-condition generation, we construct 50K composed examples with γmin=0.4\gamma_{\text{min}}=0.4, γmax=0.8\gamma_{\text{max}}=0.8, and finetune Modaliff with LoRA of rank 16 and scaling 32 for 60K iterations with a learning rate of 5e-6.

Evaluation settings

We evaluate cross-modal generation across image (I), text (T), and audio (A), using metrics for both fidelity and semantic alignment. Image fidelity is measured by FID (Heusel et al. 2017) on 256×\times256 images, using 30K MSCOCO validation samples (Lin et al. 2014) for T→\toI and VGGSound test samples for A→\toI. Text quality is evaluated with CIDEr (Vedantam, Zitnick, and Parikh 2015) on MSCOCO for I→\toT, where each image has five reference captions, and AudioCaps for A→\toT, with five captions per audio clip. Audio fidelity is measured by FAD (Kilgour et al. 2019) on AudioCaps for T→\toA and VGGSound for I→\toA. Semantic alignment is assessed using CLIP score (Radford et al. 2021) for image-text pairs, CLAP score (Wu et al. 2023) for audio-text pairs, and ImgBind score (Girdhar et al. 2023) for audio-image pairs. For multi-condition evaluation, we hold out 1K samples from the finetuning set, using γmin=0.4\gamma_{\text{min}}=0.4, γmax=0.8\gamma_{\text{max}}=0.8 to encourage semantically distinct conditions.

Baselines

We compare Modaliff against state-of-the-art specialist models and any-to-any diffusion models, including CoDi (Tang et al. 2023), OmniFlow (Li et al. 2025), and FlowBind (Cha et al. 2026). For specialists, we adopt the results from FlowBind. For any-to-any models, we use the official checkpoints, sampling scripts, recommended hyperparameters, and fixing latent generation to 50 sampling steps across all methods for a fair comparison.

4.2 Experiment Results

One-to-One Cross-Modality Generation

Tabs. 1 and 2 report fidelity and semantic alignment for one-to-one cross-modal generation across text, image, and audio, while Appdx. A.1 compares the training-data scale and trainable parameters of the generalists. We observe that Modaliff outperforms the generalists in fidelity on most generation tasks, with particularly large gains on T→\toI and T→\toA, highlighting the effectiveness of preserving modality-native token representations within a unified denoising sequence. CoDi’s inferior performance typically stems from combining multiple outdated U-Net architectures and training under a multi-task objective, making it difficult to balance learning across modalities. OmniFlow exhibits strong T→\toI alignment, which is expected given its initialization from SD3-Medium, a strong foundation model trained on billions of high-quality samples. However, OmniFlow underperforms in FID, which we attribute to the substantial amount of synthetic and stylized imagery in the training data of SD3-Medium, causing its generations to differ in visual style from the realistic images in MSCOCO. Moreover, both CoDi and OmniFlow denoise high-dimensional image and audio VAE latents (Rombach et al. 2022; Liu et al. 2023a), requiring larger denoisers and higher training cost. In contrast, Modaliff operates on compact semantic latents produced by contrastive encoders (CLIP for images and CLAP for audio), shifting low-level synthesis to frozen decoders and matching these baselines with a substantially smaller denoiser and fewer computational resources. Although FlowBind improves performance over CoDi by jointly training all velocity models with a shared latent encoder, its fixed shared vector representation discards the token-level structure of text, causing FlowBind to underperform in both text generation quality and alignment on the text-conditioned routes T→\toI and T→\toA.

When VGGSound is excluded from training, Modaliff predictably degrades on A→\toI and I→\toA, as Modaliff must learn these mappings indirectly through text rather than from direct image-audio supervision. Nevertheless, Modaliff-noVGG still outperforms CoDi on I→\toA and OmniFlow on both A→\toI and I→\toA in fidelity, while remaining comparable in alignment despite both baselines using millions of image-audio pairs, indicating that Modaliff can effectively use text as the central modality to learn image-audio generation.

Multi-Condition Generation

Tab. 3 reports multi-condition alignment for generalists and Modaliff using score composition (Sec. 3.2) and composed caption finetuning (Sec. 3.3). For each task, we measure the ImageBind score between the generated output and each condition separately. Without multi-condition training, Modaliff remains competitive with the baselines and performs particularly well on (T+I)→\toA, demonstrating that the learned one-to-one mappings can be composed effectively at inference. Finetuning with composed captions further improves five of the six alignment scores and achieves the best performance on four, confirming that language provides effective supervision for modeling interactions between conditions. The only exception is the lower A-I score of finetuned variant on (T+A)→\toI relative to Modaliff (CFG), which arises because static images are inherently limited in depicting transient acoustic events such as speaking or chirping, even when this information is preserved in the composed caption, thereby limiting their transfer from the T→\toI teacher to (T+A)→\toI mapping.

This behavior is consistent with Fig. 2, where fine-tuning improves visual quality and text alignment, while actions suggested by the audio, such as giving a speech, remain difficult to depict in a single image. For (T + I)→\toI, Fig. 3 shows that Modaliff produces higher-quality images and follows both conditions more accurately, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed finetuning strategy.

4.3 Ablation Studies

Impact of Role-based Positional Embedding

We compare role-based PE against local indexing using two Modaliff models that differ only in the positional scheme, each reduced to 159M parameters for efficiency. As shown in Figs. 4, role-based PE consistently outperforms local indexing on all generation routes, with the largest gain on text generation. We attribute this improvement to the positional conflict introduced by local indexing in the attention projections shared across all generation tasks. Under local indexing, each condition and target segment resets its positions from the same origin, creating artificial correspondences between unrelated tokens that share similar indices. The shared projections must then suppress this bias while preserving the positional structure of the target sequence, which is particularly important for text generation. Role-based PE removes these cross-segment biases by presenting condition tokens to target queries under a shared positional reference, enabling more effective routing across variable generation tasks.

Impact of the Similarity Band [γmin,γmax]\left[\gamma_{\text{min}},\gamma_{\text{max}}\right]

To evaluate similarity filtering for multi-condition triplet construction, we fix γmax=0.8\gamma_{\text{max}}=0.8 to exclude near-duplicate pairs, vary γmin∈{0,0.2,0.4,0.6}\gamma_{\text{min}}\in\left\{0,0.2,0.4,0.6\right\}, and finetune Modaliff on 10K composed samples per setting. Tab. 4 reports the alignment between the generated target and each of the two conditions across three multi-condition tasks. Across all tasks, increasing γmin\gamma_{\text{min}} improves alignment with one condition but reduces alignment with the other. This is because a high γmin\gamma_{\text{min}} retains pairs with highly similar captions, causing x~c\tilde{x}^{c} to emphasize shared content and provide limited supervision for composing distinct conditions. Conversely, a lower γmin\gamma_{\text{min}} admits more diverse pairs and strengthens the use of complementary information but may introduce details supported by only one input, thereby reducing alignment with the other. These results support our hypothesis for similarity-based filtering and we use γmin=0.4\gamma_{\text{min}}=0.4 to balance individual-condition alignment with effective multi-condition fusion.

5 Related Work

Building on the success in pairwise cross-modal generation (Liu et al. 2023a; Esser et al. 2024; Le et al. 2026), diffusion models (Song et al. 2021) have recently been extended to unified multimodal generation. Versatile Diffusion (Xu et al. 2023) extends latent diffusion into a unified image-text framework with a modular cross-modal architecture, but its model size grows with the number of modalities and the framework remains limited to the image-text setting. UniDiffuser (Bao et al. 2023b) instead models the joint distribution of all modalities using a single transformer-based noise prediction network that represents each modality as a token sequence. This design provides a general formulation for multimodality, but it requires fully aligned multimodal tuples and substantial training time. CoDi (Tang et al. 2023) extends any-to-any generation to diverse modalities, including text, image, audio, and video, through a two-stage pipeline that first learns modality-specific encoders with contrastive learning and then trains diffusion models for conditional generation. While this supports flexible and multi-source generation, it requires contrastive pretraining and multiple diffusion models whose number scales linearly with the number of modalities. OmniFlow (Li et al. 2025) replaces diffusion with flow matching to model a joint distribution across modalities and adapts a pretrained SD3 backbone (Esser et al. 2024) to reduce training cost. However, it still depends on fully aligned multimodal tuples, and missing modalities must be synthesized during training. More recently, FlowBind (Cha et al. 2026) adopts flow matching to learn a shared latent prior and modality-specific velocity models that map between the prior and each modality’s latent space. Although FlowBind jointly optimizes all models from paired data, it requires matched dimensions between the prior and modality representations, scales one model per modality, and assumes paired supervision for every modality pair.

In summary, most of existing multimodal diffusion models rely on fully aligned tuples, contrastive pretraining, or modality-specific generators whose parameters scale linearly with the number of modalities. FlowBind reduces reliance on aligned tuples through single-stage paired-data training, but couples all modalities to a shared prior’s dimensionality, uses one velocity model per modality, and assumes supervision for every modality pair. By contrast, our method learns directly from paired data, preserves modality-specific structure in native latent tokens, uses a single denoiser for all generation tasks to avoid modality-dependent parameter growth, and supports settings with missing modality pairs.

6 Conclusion

We presented Modaliff, a token-based diffusion framework for any-to-any generation that requires neither a shared representation space nor fully aligned multimodal tuples. By representing modality-native condition and target tokens under a unified token sequence, Modaliff supports diverse one-to-one and multi-condition tasks using a single denoiser trained on paired data. Extensive experiments across text, image, and audio demonstrate that Modaliff achieves the best fidelity among any-to-any models on most generation tasks while using substantially fewer parameters and training data.
